title: Non‐Linear Increases of Soil Carbon Stocks and Turnover Along Alpine Greening Gradients on Different Bedrocks
content:
Alpine warming and greening have largely unknown consequences for soil organic carbon (SOC) dynamics and the mechanisms governing sequestration potential. Along elevation gradients from subalpine forests to the periglacial zone on three bedrock types, we show that SOC stocks and radiocarbon (14C)-derived turnover times follow a non-linear sigmoidal relationship with elevation, with a distinct threshold at the vegetation line. High alpine nival soils receive negligible carbon inputs, reflected in millennia-long 14C-derived turnover times and low SOC saturation relative to SOC-stabilizing pedogenic oxides (PO). Downslope grassland soils receive higher carbon inputs and are therefore more C-saturated, driving faster turnover with little net SOC gain. We infer that SOC sequestration potential under alpine greening will be confined to areas around the vegetation line, with bedrock type modulating the magnitude of carbon uptake.


ABSTRACT

Alpine ecosystems are experiencing warming, leading to alpine greening—an upward migration and enhanced productivity of vegetation. Although soils represent the largest carbon (C) stocks in these ecosystems, impacts of greening on soil organic carbon (SOC) dynamics remain unknown, especially in the high alpine zone. We measured SOC stocks, quality and radiocarbon (14C) based turnover rates along elevation gradients from (sub)alpine forests to periglacial zones on three bedrock types, representing trajectories of changes in climate and vegetation and weathering regime. Data were linked to SOC stabilizing pedogenic oxides (PO) to assess the potential of soils to sequester C upon alpine greening. Results show pronounced decreases in SOC stocks (from 10 to 1 kg C m−2) and increases in 14C-based turnover times (from decades to millennia) with increasing elevation. This pattern followed a non-linear sigmoidal function with a threshold at the vegetation line where grassland transitions to the nival zone. High alpine soils showed low SOC:PO ratios, indicating low C saturation and a high capacity to stabilize SOC on reactive minerals. However, negligible 14C-derived carbon inputs suggest that low vegetation productivity constrains SOC sequestration in these soils. In contrast, towards lower elevation with a warmer climate, grassland soils receive higher C inputs, but appear more C saturated, leading to greater SOC turnover but little SOC stock changes. Bedrock influenced SOC dynamics with approximately 50% smaller SOC stocks and faster turnover rates in dolomitic than in siliceous soils, due to slower weathering and lower SOC stabilization. Using elevation as a space-for-time substitution, we infer that SOC sequestration under alpine greening will be confined to areas around the vegetation line, with parent material influencing the magnitude of C uptake. Future projections of SOC dynamics should account for vegetation shifts and bedrock-driven stabilization to constrain the role of alpine soils in land carbon-climate feedbacks.
